posts.summary:

The first is a quick survey about how people use AI in their work and studies. Everyone who completes the survey enters a random draw to win an Apple iPhone Duo.

The second offer gives community members one month of Wispr Pro on desktop for free.
posts.body:
The best part? The survey takes approximately one minute, while the Wispr offer lets you explore voice-powered productivity and AI-assisted development.

🎁 TWO OPPORTUNITIES TO CHECK OUT

📱 iPhone Duo: Complete a short AI survey to enter the prize draw.

🎙️ Wispr Pro: Claim one month of desktop Pro access through the offer.

💻 Target audience: Developers, students, and technology enthusiasts.

Let's understand how both opportunities work and how you can participate.

📱 1. Win an iPhone Duo With a 1-Minute AI Survey

WeMakeDevs is collecting information about how people use artificial intelligence in their work and studies.

The survey asks about everyday AI usage and helps the team understand how the developer community uses AI tools.

🎁 What Is the Reward?

The email advertises an Apple iPhone Duo, valued at approximately ₹3 lakh.

According to the announcement, one winner will be selected randomly from the people who complete the survey.

Here's what you need to know:

📱 Prize: Apple iPhone Duo.

⏱️ Time required: Approximately one minute.

📝 Task: Complete the AI usage survey.

🏆 Winner selection: Random draw.

🎯 Eligibility: Subject to the survey's official terms.

Important: Completing the survey does not guarantee that you will win the phone. It enters you into the draw, and the winner is selected randomly.

🚀 How to Enter the Giveaway

Step 1: Open the survey link provided in the WeMakeDevs email.

Take the WeMakeDevs AI Survey

Step 2: Answer the questions honestly about how you use AI.

Step 3: Submit the survey.

Step 4: Watch your email for updates from WeMakeDevs regarding the winner announcement.

The email says the winner will be announced the following week. Check the original announcement for any updated dates or additional conditions.

⚠️ Is the iPhone Guaranteed?

No. This is a giveaway, not a participation reward.

You don't need to buy anything according to the email, but you should read any official terms associated with the survey before submitting your information.

Never share passwords, banking PINs, or OTPs to claim a giveaway prize.

🎙️ 2. Get One Month of Wispr Pro for FREE

The second opportunity may be particularly useful if you regularly write code, prepare documentation, send emails, or work with AI assistants.

WeMakeDevs has announced one month of Wispr Pro on desktop for its community members.

Wispr Flow is a voice-to-text tool that converts natural speech into polished text in the applications you use on your computer.

Instead of typing every sentence, you can speak your thoughts and let Wispr Flow transcribe and clean them up.

💻 What Is Wispr Flow?

Wispr Flow is designed to make writing and computer-based communication faster using voice.

You speak naturally, and it converts your speech into text while handling filler words, repeated phrases, and formatting.

You can use it for activities such as:

✉️ Writing emails.

📝 Preparing documentation.

💻 Dictating coding prompts.

🔍 Explaining bugs to AI coding assistants.

📋 Writing project updates.

💬 Preparing messages and team communications.

📚 Taking notes while studying.

For developers, one particularly useful application is explaining a complicated coding requirement to an AI assistant without manually typing a long prompt.

🎁 What Does the Offer Include?

According to the WeMakeDevs email:

Duration: One month.

Product: Wispr Pro on desktop.

Platform: Laptop or desktop computer.

Cost of the promotional month: Free, according to the offer.

The email specifically instructs users to sign up using their laptop or desktop computer to claim the offer.

🚀 How to Claim Your Free Month

Step 1: Open the offer from your WeMakeDevs email.

Claim One Month of Wispr Pro

Step 2: Open the link on your laptop or desktop computer.

Step 3: Follow the signup instructions.

Step 4: Check that the promotional offer is applied to your account before using the service.

Step 5: Try Wispr Flow in your usual applications, such as your code editor, email client, or AI assistant.

Review the offer's terms for any billing details, renewal conditions, and eligibility requirements before activating it.

🤖 Why Should Developers Try Wispr Flow?

If you use AI tools for programming, you probably know how long it can take to explain a complex feature or bug in writing.

Voice input can help you communicate those details more quickly.

Example: Writing an AI Coding Prompt

Instead of manually typing:

Create a REST API for managing products.
Include CRUD operations, validation,
exception handling, and database integration.

You can speak your requirements naturally and let Wispr Flow convert them into text.

You can then review the result and send it to your preferred coding assistant.

Other Useful Applications

For students:

Prepare study notes.

Summarize ideas in your own words.

Draft project documentation.

For developers:

Explain implementation requirements.

Write bug reports.

Document APIs.

Prepare pull request descriptions.

For content creators:

Draft video scripts.

Brainstorm blog ideas.

Prepare social media captions.

Dictate outlines for articles.

Remember that voice transcription should still be reviewed for technical accuracy, especially when working with code, commands, or sensitive information.

🔥 Which Opportunity Should You Try First?

You can explore both offers because they serve different purposes.

📱 If You Want to Try for the iPhone

Complete the AI usage survey and review the giveaway conditions.

Your entry gives you a chance to win, but the final outcome depends on the random draw.

🎙️ If You Want a Productivity Tool

Claim the Wispr Pro offer on your desktop computer and test how voice typing fits into your workflow.

This offer provides a defined period of access rather than a competitive prize draw.

💡 My Recommendation

If you are interested in both, complete the short survey first, then claim the Wispr offer.

That way, you can enter the giveaway and explore a useful productivity tool without confusing the two rewards.

⚠️ Important Things to Remember

Before participating, keep these points in mind:

The iPhone giveaway has one randomly selected winner according to the email.

Survey completion does not guarantee a phone.

The Wispr offer is for one month of desktop Pro access.

Use a laptop or desktop to claim the Wispr offer, as instructed.

Check the offer terms for eligibility and subscription renewal details.

Use the original WeMakeDevs email or official channels to verify the offers.

Never pay an unofficial agent to claim either opportunity.

🏁 Final Verdict

WeMakeDevs has shared two opportunities worth exploring if you're part of the developer community.

📱 iPhone Duo Giveaway: Complete a short AI survey and enter the random draw for the advertised phone.

🎙️ Free Wispr Pro Month: Claim one month of desktop access and explore voice-powered writing, documentation, and AI-assisted development.

Neither opportunity should be confused with a guaranteed physical reward for every participant.

posts.title: 🚨 WIN $100 FOR YOUR HACKATHON PROJECT! 💰 | MLH × DEV Writing Challenge October 2026 | Submit Now!
posts.summary:
Built something cool at a hackathon but don't know what to do next? Here's an opportunity to give your project a second chance to shine! 🚀

The October MLH × DEV Writing Challenge 2026 invites developers to write about projects they built at Major League Hacking (MLH) events and publish their stories on DEV Community.

And the exciting part? Selected projects can win $100 each! 💵

You don't necessarily need to build another project from scratch. If you've already participated in an eligible MLH hackathon, you can share what you built, explain how it works, discuss the challenges you faced, and tell the community what you learned.
posts.body:
💰 REWARD: $100 PER SELECTED PROJECT

📅 Challenge period: October 1–31, 2026

✍️ Platform: DEV Community

🏆 Selection: DEV editorial team

🏷️ Required hashtag: #mlhacks

Important: This is a competitive writing challenge, not a guaranteed reward for everyone who publishes an article.

🚀 What Is the MLH × DEV Writing Challenge?

The MLH × DEV Writing Challenge is a monthly initiative that encourages developers to document and share projects created at MLH hackathons.

Hackathons often last only a weekend, but the learning continues long after the event ends.

You might have built an AI tool, a productivity application, a web platform, a mobile application, or an experimental project with your team.

This challenge gives you an opportunity to turn that experience into a useful technical article that other developers can learn from.

Your article can explain:

💡 The problem you wanted to solve.

🛠️ The technologies you used.

💻 How you built your project.

🧩 The biggest challenges you faced.

🚀 What makes your solution interesting.

📚 What you learned during the hackathon.

The goal is to help other developers understand your project while showcasing your technical work and creativity.

💰 What Can You Win?

The official challenge page advertises $100 per selected project.

The DEV editorial team will select at least one favourite project each month. Additional projects may also be selected, depending on the number of submissions.

Selection considers several factors:

Technical substance: Does your article demonstrate meaningful technical work?

Originality: Is your project interesting, creative, or different?

Clear storytelling: Can readers understand what you built and why?

Community popularity: Does your post attract genuine interest and discussion?

There is no fixed guarantee that every participant will win.

The best strategy is to write an article that provides real value instead of simply promoting your project.

📅 Important Dates

The October challenge runs from:

Start: October 1, 2026

Deadline: October 31, 2026

Platform: DEV Community

Reward: $100 per selected project

The challenge window follows Eastern Time, so check the official page for the exact closing time.

If you have already built an eligible project at an MLH hackathon, start preparing your article now rather than waiting until the final day.

🎯 Who Can Participate?

This challenge is particularly relevant to developers who have built projects at MLH hackathons.

You may have created:

🤖 An AI-powered application.

🌐 A website or web application.

📱 A mobile application.

⚙️ An automation tool.

🔐 A cybersecurity project.

📊 A data analysis or visualization tool.

🧠 An experimental application using new technologies.

The key requirement is that your project must have been built at an MLH hackathon.

Simply writing about an unrelated personal project does not meet the stated participation process.

If you're unsure whether your event qualifies, check the official challenge page and its participation terms.

✍️ How to Participate — Step by Step

Step 1: Choose Your MLH Hackathon Project

Start with a project you built at an MLH event.

Choose something you can explain clearly, including its purpose, implementation, and the challenges you encountered.

Your project doesn't need to be perfect. Experimental projects and unusual ideas are welcome.

Step 2: Open the Official DEV Submission Template

The challenge page provides an official submission template to help you structure your article.

Use it to organize your project story and ensure you cover the important details.

Start from the DEV Community website and navigate to the official October MLH × DEV Writing Challenge page to access the template.

Step 3: Explain What You Built

Begin with a clear introduction.

Explain the problem, why it matters, and how your application addresses it.

Avoid starting with a long list of technologies without explaining what your project actually does.

Step 4: Describe Your Tech Stack

Tell readers which tools and technologies you used.

For example:

Java or Python for backend development.

React for the frontend.

PostgreSQL or another database.

APIs for external integrations.

AI models for intelligent features.

Cloud platforms for deployment.

Only mention technologies that you genuinely used in your project.

Step 5: Explain How It Works

Describe the architecture, workflow, or important features.

You can include screenshots, diagrams, code snippets, and links to your public repository or demo when appropriate.

Make sure the article is easy to follow for someone who hasn't seen your project before.

Step 6: Share the Challenges and Lessons

Explain what went wrong, how you debugged issues, and what you learned.

Honest technical lessons often make an article more valuable than a story that presents everything as effortless.

Step 7: Publish on DEV

Publish your article on DEV Community during the October challenge window.

Remember to include the required hashtag: #mlhacks.

Follow the official template and any additional participation requirements listed on the challenge page.

Step 8: Share Your Article

Once your post is live, share it with your teammates, friends, developer communities, and social media audience.

Genuine discussion and engagement can help more people discover your work.

Don't use fake engagement or spam communities. Focus on sharing the article with people who may find it useful.

📝 How to Write an Article That Stands Out

Want to improve your chances of being selected? Focus on the quality of your story.

1. Start With the Problem

Explain the problem your project solves and why you chose it.

2. Show the Actual Project

Include screenshots or a demonstration where possible.

Help readers understand the user experience and the outcome.

3. Explain the Technical Decisions

Discuss why you chose your architecture, database, framework, or APIs.

Mention alternatives you considered and any trade-offs you made.

4. Share Real Challenges

Explain bugs, limitations, integration problems, or time constraints you encountered during the hackathon.

Describe how you approached them.

5. Include a Demo or Repository

If permitted and available, link to your project repository or live demo so readers can explore your work.

6. Make It Easy to Read

Use short paragraphs, descriptive Markdown headings, bullet lists, and code blocks only when they help explain your implementation.

7. End With What You Learned

Summarize your main lessons and explain what you would improve if you continued developing the project.

💡 Example Article Structure

You can organize your post using this outline:

# How We Built [Project Name] at an MLH Hackathon

## What We Built

Explain the project and the problem it solves.

## Why We Built It

Describe the motivation behind the idea.

## Tech Stack

List the technologies used.

## How It Works

Explain the architecture and workflow.

## Challenges We Faced

Discuss technical problems and solutions.

## What We Learned

Share the most valuable lessons.

## What's Next?

Describe future improvements.

#mlhacks

Use this as a starting point and adapt it to your actual project.

⚠️ Important Rules to Remember

Before submitting your article, make sure you:

Participate with a project built at an MLH hackathon.

Publish your post on DEV Community within the challenge window.

Explain what you built, how it works, and what you learned.

Include #mlhacks.

Follow the official submission template.

Share your post to help people discover your work.

Read the official terms and any updates about eligibility and badges.

Don't assume that publishing an article automatically earns $100. The editorial team selects projects based on the published criteria.

🏁 Final Verdict

The October MLH × DEV Writing Challenge 2026 is a great opportunity to turn your hackathon experience into a technical article that helps other developers.

You can showcase your skills, share your learning, build your presence in the developer community, and compete for $100 per selected project.

🔥 Quick Recap

🚀 Challenge: MLH × DEV Writing Challenge

📅 Deadline: October 31, 2026

✍️ Platform: DEV Community

💰 Reward: $100 per selected project

🏷️ Required hashtag: #mlhacks

🛠️ Requirement: Write about a project built at an MLH hackathon

🏆 Selection: DEV editorial team

🚨 Ready to Submit?

If you've built something at an MLH hackathon, don't let your project story disappear after the event.

Document your work, explain what you learned, publish your article, and share it with the developer community.

BUILD → DOCUMENT → PUBLISH → SHARE → COMPETE! 🚀

For more hackathons, developer challenges, open-source opportunities, internships, and tech updates, follow Btecky. 💻

🌎 What Is GitHub Universe 2026?

GitHub Universe is GitHub's flagship developer conference, bringing together developers, open-source maintainers, technology leaders, security professionals, and builders from around the world.

The event explores how developers can work with AI, build better software, improve productivity, and collaborate on projects more effectively.

Whether you're learning to code, working as a software engineer, or building your own startup, GitHub Universe is an opportunity to discover new ideas and technologies.

🚀 Why Should You Attend?

Here are some reasons to consider registering:

Learn about the latest GitHub announcements.

Explore AI-powered software development.

Discover new developer tools and workflows.

Learn from technical presentations and demonstrations.

Understand how AI agents are changing coding.

Get ideas for your next personal or open-source project.

🎤 1. Keynote Presentations

Watch keynote presentations covering GitHub's vision, product announcements, and the future of software development.

The event website lists in-person tickets as sold out.

The physical experience includes opportunities for attendees to meet other developers, participate in sessions, explore demonstrations, and interact with sponsors and technology communities.

Register for GitHub Universe 2026

Event: GitHub Universe 2026

🤖 What Topics Should Developers Look Forward To?

GitHub Universe is especially relevant if you're interested in modern software development.

1. AI-Powered Development

Discover how AI tools can help developers write, understand, test, and maintain code.

2. AI Agents

Explore how agents can move beyond answering questions to completing multi-step tasks within software development workflows.

posts.title: What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)? A Practical Guide
posts.summary: A complete practical guide to Retrieval-Augmented Generation: document ingestion, chunking, embeddings, retrieval, reranking, grounded generation, evaluation, security and a small project architecture.
posts.body:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a way to build AI applications that answer questions using information from a collection of documents. Instead of relying only on what a language model learned during training, a RAG system searches a knowledge source at question time and supplies relevant passages to the model. The model then uses those passages to prepare an answer.

RAG is useful for internal knowledge assistants, product documentation search, support tools, policy lookup, research workflows and learning applications. It is not a guarantee of correctness: the quality of the answer depends on the quality of the documents, retrieval process, access controls and evaluation.

## 1. Why use RAG?

A language model's training data may be incomplete, outdated or unrelated to your private documents. Fine-tuning can change model behaviour, but it is not usually the best way to keep a frequently changing knowledge base current. RAG addresses a different problem: it retrieves external evidence for each request.

For example, imagine a company has hundreds of product manuals. A user asks, “Does the mobile app support offline exports?” The application searches the manuals for relevant passages, provides the strongest matches to the model, and asks it to answer using those sources. If no manual mentions offline exports, the system should say that the available documentation does not establish an answer.

### RAG compared with a normal prompt

A normal prompt includes the question and whatever context a developer manually adds. RAG adds a search stage that selects context dynamically. This is especially useful when the collection is too large to fit into every request.

## 2. The main stages of a RAG pipeline

A production pipeline usually has an ingestion path and a question-answering path.

### Stage A: Ingest and prepare documents

Collect permitted source files, extract text, preserve headings and metadata, and normalize the content. Keep useful information such as document title, URL, owner, version, publication date and access permissions.

Do not discard source identity. A retrieved passage should be traceable to the document and section from which it came. If the source is updated or deleted, your index needs a way to reflect that change.

### Stage B: Split documents into chunks

A chunk is a smaller section of a document that can be embedded and retrieved independently. Very large chunks may contain several unrelated topics. Very small chunks may lose the context needed to interpret a sentence.

A practical starting point is to split around headings or paragraphs, then apply a token-based size limit. A small overlap between neighbouring chunks can preserve context across boundaries, but excessive overlap creates duplicate results and wastes storage.

There is no universal best chunk size. Test it with the questions users actually ask. A code reference, a legal policy, and a tutorial may need different chunking strategies.

### Stage C: Create embeddings

An embedding model converts a piece of text into a numerical vector. Texts with related meaning can have vectors that are close under a chosen similarity measure. The application stores each vector alongside the original text and metadata.

Embeddings support semantic retrieval: a question can find a passage even when it uses different wording. They do not understand the document in the same way a human does, and similarity alone does not prove that a passage answers the question.

### Stage D: Retrieve relevant passages

At question time, the application embeds the query and searches the vector index. It may also use keyword search. Hybrid retrieval can help when exact product names, error codes, identifiers or technical terms matter.

The initial search may return more passages than the model needs. A reranker can score the candidates against the question and move the most relevant passages to the top. Keep the final context concise enough to leave room for instructions and the answer.

### Stage E: Generate an evidence-based answer

The application sends the question, selected passages and clear instructions to the model. Tell it to distinguish evidence from inference, cite the supplied source identifiers, and say when the sources do not contain the answer.

The model should not be allowed to treat instructions embedded inside retrieved documents as trusted application instructions. Retrieved text is data. This is an important prompt-injection boundary.

## 3. A simple architecture

A small system can be represented as:

1. **Ingestion:** read documents and extract text.
2. **Preparation:** clean, split and attach metadata.
3. **Indexing:** create embeddings and store vectors.
4. **Query:** accept a user's question.
5. **Retrieval:** find candidate passages using semantic and/or keyword search.
6. **Reranking:** prioritize the most useful candidates.
7. **Generation:** ask the language model to answer from the selected evidence.
8. **Validation:** check citations, permissions, format and answer quality.
9. **Monitoring:** record retrieval quality, latency, cost and failure patterns.

Keep ingestion separate from answering. This makes it possible to update the index when documents change without rebuilding the whole application for every question.

## 4. Build a small course-notes assistant

Start with five to ten documents that you are allowed to use. Choose a narrow subject, such as a course module or a product's public documentation.

### Step 1: Prepare the source set

Give each document a stable identifier. Extract text and preserve headings. Remove repeated navigation text and boilerplate, but do not remove warnings, dates or qualifications that change the meaning.

### Step 2: Create chunks

Split by section first and then by a token budget. Store metadata with every chunk:

- document ID and title
- section heading
- source URL or file name
- last updated date
- access-control label
- chunk sequence number

### Step 3: Index and retrieve

Create embeddings for each chunk and store them in a vector index. When a question arrives, retrieve a small candidate set. Inspect the results manually before connecting a language model. If the right source is not retrieved, generation cannot reliably fix that failure.

### Step 4: Add grounded generation

Pass the retrieved passages with explicit source labels. Ask for a concise answer and citations that refer to those labels. If the evidence is missing or contradictory, require the assistant to explain the limitation rather than invent a resolution.

### Step 5: Test with a fixed question set

Create questions whose answers are present, questions that require combining two passages, questions with ambiguous wording, and questions that are not answered by the documents. Check both the retrieved evidence and the final response.

## 5. How to evaluate RAG properly

RAG has at least two separate quality problems: retrieval and generation.

**Retrieval evaluation** asks whether the system found the right evidence. Useful measures include recall at K (whether a relevant passage appears in the first K results), precision at K (how many of those results are relevant), and ranking quality.

**Answer evaluation** asks whether the generated response is supported by the retrieved material, complete enough for the question, readable, and appropriately cautious. Check whether citations actually support the statements beside them.

Track additional operational measures: response latency, embedding and model cost, index freshness, failure rate, and the number of requests where no useful source was found. Review real failure examples; a single average score can hide important problems.

## 6. Common RAG problems and fixes

| Problem | Likely cause | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correct document is never retrieved | Weak chunking, metadata or query match | Inspect chunks; add keyword or hybrid search |
| Relevant result is ranked too low | Similar passages dominate | Test a reranker and tune candidate count |
| Answer includes unsupported details | Prompt allows speculation or context is weak | Require evidence and explicit uncertainty |
| Answer misses a key qualification | Chunk split removed surrounding context | Use heading-aware chunks and limited overlap |
| Results contain outdated facts | Index was not refreshed | Add update and deletion workflows |
| Private content appears to the wrong user | Permissions were not enforced during retrieval | Filter by access rights before generation |
| Costs rise unexpectedly | Too many large chunks are sent | Rerank, deduplicate and limit final context |

## 7. Security and privacy considerations

RAG does not remove the need for application security. Apply document permissions before a passage reaches the model. Do not retrieve every document and rely on the model to decide which user may see it.

Treat source documents as untrusted input. A document could contain text that attempts to manipulate the assistant or request secret data. Keep system instructions separate, restrict tools, validate actions in application code, and never put credentials in retrieved content.

Consider retention, deletion, data residency and provider policies before indexing sensitive information. When a source document is removed or a user's access changes, update the index and caches accordingly.

## 8. When RAG is not the right answer

RAG is not required for every AI feature. If the task is a small transformation that needs no external knowledge, a normal prompt may be simpler. If the task requires exact database records or transactional updates, a structured API or database query may be more appropriate than semantic search.

If the desired behaviour is a consistent style or a specialized task pattern, prompt design or fine-tuning may be relevant. RAG and fine-tuning solve different problems and can also be combined.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does RAG eliminate hallucinations?

No. It can provide relevant evidence and make answers easier to verify, but retrieval can fail and models can misinterpret sources. Evaluate grounding and provide a safe “not found” behaviour.

### Do I need a vector database?

Not always. A small prototype can use a local index or a search engine with vector support. Choose infrastructure based on data size, filtering, operational needs and team experience.

### Should I use only vector search?

Not necessarily. Keyword search is valuable for exact names, IDs and error messages. Hybrid retrieval is often worth testing.

### How often should the index be updated?

Update it whenever source freshness matters. For frequently changing documents, use an incremental pipeline that handles additions, edits and deletions.

## Final checklist

- Use documents you are authorized to index.
- Preserve source identifiers, dates and permissions.
- Test chunking with realistic questions.
- Inspect retrieval results before tuning generation.
- Keep the final context focused and within the model's token budget.
- Require grounded answers and traceable citations.
- Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
- Monitor freshness, access control, cost and latency.

The best RAG system is not the one with the most complicated vector database. It is the smallest system that reliably finds the right evidence, respects permissions, and clearly communicates what the sources do and do not say.

posts.title: LLMs Explained: Tokens, Context Windows, and Temperature
posts.summary: A practical, in-depth guide to tokenization, context-window budgeting, temperature, sampling controls, and experiments for building more reliable LLM applications.
posts.body:
A large language model (LLM) can write an explanation, summarize a document, generate code, or answer a question because it has learned statistical patterns in language and other training data. To use one well, however, you need to understand three practical controls: **tokens**, the **context window**, and **temperature**. They affect how much information a model can process and how it chooses what to generate.

This guide explains each concept from the ground up, shows how they interact, and walks through a small experiment you can run when building an AI feature.

## 1. What is a token?

A token is a unit of text processed by a language model. It is not always a complete word. Depending on the tokenizer, a token may represent a whole short word, part of a longer word, punctuation, whitespace, or a frequently occurring character sequence.

For example, a sentence such as:

> The model reads text as tokens, not as a simple count of words.

might be split into pieces that do not line up exactly with the words you see. The exact split depends on the model's tokenizer. Two sentences with the same number of words can therefore use different numbers of tokens.

### Why do models use tokens?

Neural language models operate on numerical representations. A tokenizer converts text into token IDs, and the model processes those IDs. During generation, the model produces token IDs that are converted back into readable text.

Tokens are used because they provide a manageable vocabulary of reusable pieces. A model does not need a separate vocabulary entry for every possible name, spelling, or word form. It can combine smaller pieces to represent unfamiliar terms.

### What affects token count?

- **Word length and spelling:** uncommon or long words may split into several tokens.
- **Punctuation and formatting:** code, symbols, JSON, and URLs can tokenize differently from ordinary prose.
- **Language:** token efficiency varies across languages and writing systems.
- **Repeated patterns:** common phrases and familiar text structures may use fewer tokens than unusual strings.

A rough words-to-tokens estimate can help with planning, but it is not a reliable billing or capacity calculation. Use the tokenizer associated with the model you are actually calling when exact counts matter.

### Input tokens and output tokens

An API request can contain input tokens and generate output tokens. Input may include the system instructions, developer instructions, user message, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results, and formatting requirements. Output tokens are the generated response.

Many services account for input and output separately, and some models have different limits for each. Always check the current model documentation and pricing rather than assuming that every token has the same cost.

## 2. What is a context window?

The context window is the amount of tokenized information a model can consider in a single interaction or generation request. Think of it as the model's working space for the current task.

It may contain more than the latest question. Depending on the application, the context can include:

1. Instructions that define the assistant's role and boundaries.
2. The user's current request.
3. Earlier messages that are still included in the conversation.
4. Documents or passages retrieved from a knowledge base.
5. Tool results, such as database records or search output.
6. The space reserved for the model's answer.

### A simple context-budget example

Imagine an application has a context limit of 16,000 tokens. Its request might allocate approximately:

| Part of the request | Example token budget |
| --- | ---: |
| Instructions and response rules | 1,000 |
| Conversation history | 3,000 |
| Retrieved reference material | 7,000 |
| Current user question | 500 |
| Reserved answer space | 2,000 |
| Remaining headroom | 2,500 |

These figures are illustrative, not a recommendation or a limit for a particular model. The important point is that retrieved content and conversation history consume space too. If an application fills the entire context with source documents, it may leave too little room for a useful answer.

### A larger context is not automatically better

A large context window can make it possible to work with longer documents or more history, but it does not guarantee that every detail will be used correctly. A model can overlook a relevant passage, confuse similar facts, or produce an answer that is not supported by the supplied material.

Long prompts can also increase latency and cost. Sending an entire knowledge base with every question is usually wasteful. A better design retrieves a small set of relevant passages, preserves their source identifiers, and asks the model to answer from that evidence.

### What happens when the context is too large?

The application or model service may reject the request, truncate content, or require the application to shorten the input. The exact behaviour depends on the API and model. Do not rely on silent truncation: handle token-limit errors and make the context-building process explicit.

Common ways to manage context include:

- **Summarization:** retain a compact summary of older conversation turns.
- **Retrieval:** search for relevant passages instead of attaching every document.
- **Chunking:** split long documents into sections that can be retrieved independently.
- **Filtering:** remove duplicate, stale, or unrelated material before sending it.
- **Output budgeting:** reserve enough space for the answer and any required structured output.

## 3. What is temperature?

Temperature is a generation setting that changes how strongly a model favours higher-probability next-token choices. A lower temperature generally makes the distribution more concentrated around likely choices. A higher temperature generally allows more variation among plausible choices.

It is useful to think of temperature as a control over variation, not as a dial for intelligence.

### Low and high temperature in practice

Suppose a model is asked to suggest a title for a beginner's Python tutorial.

- With a **lower temperature**, it may repeatedly choose familiar, direct wording such as “Python Lists for Beginners.”
- With a **higher temperature**, it may offer a wider range of phrasing, metaphors, or creative angles.

Neither setting guarantees correctness. A low-temperature answer can still contain a factual error, and a high-temperature answer can still be accurate. Temperature does not verify sources or make a model understand a task more deeply.

### When should you use a lower temperature?

Lower variation is often useful when outputs should be consistent, such as:

- Extracting fields into a defined JSON structure.
- Classifying support tickets into a fixed set of categories.
- Rewriting text to follow a stable style guide.
- Producing repeatable responses for a narrow workflow.

You should still validate the output in code. If a field must be a date, number, or permitted category, check it rather than trusting the model to comply.

### When might a higher temperature help?

More variation can be useful for brainstorming, naming, creative writing, or generating several alternative approaches. It can help avoid receiving nearly identical suggestions every time.

For a task that requires factual answers, increasing temperature is not a substitute for better evidence. Improve the prompt, retrieval quality, source material, and evaluation process first.

## 4. Temperature is not the only sampling control

Some model APIs expose other generation parameters, such as top-p or output-token limits. Availability and exact behaviour vary by model.

**Top-p (nucleus sampling)** limits the candidate set to tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a chosen threshold. Temperature and top-p both affect sampling, but they do so in different ways. Avoid changing several sampling parameters at once when you are trying to understand their effect.

An output-token limit controls how much the model may generate. It is different from the context window: one is a generation budget, while the other is the overall working context. A response can stop because it reaches its output limit even when the input context itself was valid.

Some reasoning-oriented models may expose different controls or ignore settings that other models support. Check the documentation for the exact model and API version you use.

## 5. How tokens, context, and temperature work together

Consider a documentation assistant that answers questions about a software project.

1. The user asks, “How do I configure the database connection?”
2. The application searches the project's documentation.
3. It selects a few relevant passages and includes their source names.
4. The instructions tell the model to answer only from those passages and say when the documentation is incomplete.
5. The model generates a response within the reserved output budget.

Tokens determine how much of the instructions, question, history, and retrieved documentation fit. The context window sets the overall capacity for that request. Temperature influences how varied the generated wording may be.

These controls solve different problems. Increasing the context window does not improve retrieval. Lowering temperature does not make missing documentation appear. Increasing the output limit does not make a response more accurate.

## 6. A practical experiment you can run

You can learn more by changing one variable at a time.

### Step 1: Prepare a fixed prompt

Use the same task and source material for every run. For example:

> Explain the difference between an input token and an output token. Use only the supplied notes. If the notes do not contain an answer, say so.

Keep the model, prompt, and source notes unchanged during the first comparison.

### Step 2: Compare generation settings

Run the prompt with a low temperature and then with a higher temperature, if the selected model supports that setting. Save both responses. Compare factual consistency, wording variation, completeness, and whether either response adds unsupported claims.

Do not judge only by which answer sounds better. Check each statement against the source notes.

### Step 3: Test context size

Create a short source document and a longer one containing relevant and irrelevant sections. Ask the same question. Observe whether the application retrieves the right material and whether the answer cites the correct section.

If the longer document performs worse, investigate retrieval and context construction before simply increasing the context limit.

### Step 4: Record results

Keep a small table with the model name, settings, approximate input and output token counts, latency, cost, and evaluation result. This makes changes measurable and helps you reproduce a good configuration later.

## 7. Common mistakes and how to avoid them

| Mistake | Why it causes trouble | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treating one word as one token | Tokenization varies by text and language | Use the model's tokenizer for exact estimates |
| Sending every document on every request | Wastes context, time, and cost | Retrieve only relevant passages |
| Assuming a large context guarantees recall | The model can still miss or confuse details | Test retrieval and answer quality separately |
| Raising temperature to improve accuracy | Temperature changes variation, not factual grounding | Improve evidence and validation |
| Setting the output limit too low | Useful answers may be cut off | Reserve a realistic output budget |
| Changing many settings at once | You cannot identify what caused a difference | Run controlled experiments |

## 8. Design checklist for a real application

Before shipping an LLM feature, make sure you can answer these questions:

- Which model and tokenizer are being used?
- What information is included in the prompt, and why?
- How are older messages summarized or removed?
- How are documents retrieved, chunked, and ranked?
- Is there enough context space for the answer?
- Is the output limit appropriate for the task?
- Does the model support the sampling settings you are configuring?
- Are outputs validated before they trigger an action?
- Do you have representative test cases for normal, edge, and unsupported questions?
- Do you measure quality, latency, and cost after every meaningful change?

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a token the same as a word?

No. A token can be a complete word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text unit. The number of tokens in a sentence depends on its wording and tokenizer.

### Does a bigger context window make an LLM smarter?

No. It gives the model room to process more input, but it does not guarantee that the model will identify or use every relevant detail correctly.

### Does temperature zero guarantee the same answer every time?

Not necessarily. Behaviour can depend on the model, serving infrastructure, and other settings. A low temperature usually reduces variation, but it is not a universal guarantee of deterministic output.

### Which temperature is best for coding?

There is no single best value for every coding task. Start with the model provider's recommended defaults, use a controlled test set, and validate generated code with tests, static analysis, and review.

### Can I increase the context window by shortening the prompt?

You cannot change the model's advertised context limit that way, but you can fit more useful information within the available budget by removing repetition, summarizing history, and retrieving only relevant source material.

## Key takeaways

- **Tokens** are the units the model processes; they are not identical to words or characters.
- The **context window** is the working space for instructions, history, retrieved content, the question, and the answer.
- **Temperature** influences output variation; it is not a factuality or intelligence setting.
- Retrieval, context management, output budgeting, and evaluation are as important as model settings.
- Measure changes with a fixed test set instead of relying on a few impressive demonstrations.

When you build with LLMs, begin with a small, measurable workflow. Understand what goes into the prompt, keep only useful context, validate the result, and consult the current documentation for the exact model and API you deploy.

posts.title: How to Build Real Projects Instead of Only Following Tutorials
posts.summary: A practical beginner-friendly guide to how to build real projects instead of only following tutorials, with key concepts, a learning workflow, common mistakes, and next steps.
posts.body:
## The idea in plain English

How to Build Real Projects Instead of Only Following Tutorials is easier to understand when you connect the concept to a real problem. In software development, the goal is not to learn a tool because it is popular; it is to understand what it solves, what trade-offs it introduces, and when a simpler option is enough.

This guide introduces the core idea, the vocabulary you will encounter, and a practical way to begin. Treat the examples as learning patterns and check the official documentation for version-specific behavior before using them in production.

## Why it matters

Developers work with systems made of smaller components. A clear mental model helps you decide where a component belongs, how it communicates with the rest of the application, and how to debug it when something fails. It also helps you explain your design choices during code reviews and interviews.

For a beginner, focus on three questions:

- **Problem:** What pain point does this approach address?
- **Mechanism:** What happens step by step when it runs?
- **Trade-off:** What extra complexity, cost, or maintenance does it add?

## A practical learning workflow

1. Start with a tiny example that demonstrates one concept.
2. Run it locally and observe the output rather than copying code blindly.
3. Change one input or configuration value and predict what will happen.
4. Add error handling and test an invalid input.
5. Write down what you learned and the limits of the example.

For example, when exploring how to build real projects instead of only following tutorials, create a small project with one responsibility. Keep configuration explicit, use meaningful names, and add a short README explaining how to run it. Small experiments make errors easier to understand than a large project assembled all at once.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Choosing a tool before defining the problem.
- Copying snippets without checking their assumptions or version.
- Ignoring security, performance, accessibility, or failure cases.
- Treating a tutorial as proof that a solution is production-ready.
- Skipping documentation and tests.

## What to learn next

After you understand the basics, build a small end-to-end project and document the decisions you made. Compare at least one alternative, test edge cases, and consult the official documentation for the framework or platform you use. That process builds durable skill—not just familiarity with terminology.

## Further reading

Start with the official documentation for the relevant language, framework, or platform. Prefer primary documentation and maintained standards over undated social posts. This article is an evergreen learning guide, not a report of a newly announced product release.

posts.body:
🏆 What Is Seva First Innovation Challenge 2026?

The Seva First Innovation Challenge (SFIC) 2026 is an innovation platform that encourages young innovators and eligible organizations to identify real problems and develop practical solutions.

The challenge brings together:

🎓 Students

🔬 Researchers

🚀 Startups

🏢 Industries

🏫 Educational institutions

🧑‍💻 Innovators

🏛️ Government organizations

👨‍🏫 Mentors and experts

The objective is simple:

Observe a real problem → Build an innovative solution → Test it → Create real-world impact.

The challenge was launched at Delhi Technological University (DTU) on September 19, 2026.

💰 ₹2 CRORE PRIZE POOL!

This is the part everyone wants to know about. 👀

The official DTU SEVA 2026 portal lists a total award pool of ₹2 Crore.

🏆 Grand Challenge Innovation Grants & Awards

💰 Total Prize Money: ₹2 Crore

But the challenge isn't only about the cash prizes.

Participants can also get opportunities for:

🧑‍🏫 Expert mentorship

🔬 Laboratory and maker-space access

🛠️ Prototype development

🏢 Industry interaction

🏛️ Government connections

🚀 Incubation support

🌍 National-level recognition

🤝 Networking opportunities

So even if you don't win the top prize, progressing through the challenge can provide valuable exposure and support.

🔥 What Are the Main Innovation Areas?

SEVA First 2026 currently has two broad innovation directions.

🇮🇳 1. National-Level Innovation

This track focuses on major national challenges.

Areas include:

🛡️ Defence

🚀 Space

🔐 National Security

🚨 Disaster Management

🤖 Artificial Intelligence

🦾 Robotics

🏭 Manufacturing

⚡ Energy

🌱 Environment

🏗️ Infrastructure

🚗 Future Mobility

If your idea can address a large-scale national problem, this could be the direction to explore.

🌱 2. Local Community-Level Innovation

You can also focus on problems affecting local communities.

Potential areas include:

🌾 Agriculture & Rural Development

📚 Education

🏥 Healthcare

🏙️ Urban Problems

🌱 Environment

🏃 Sports

💼 Employment & Livelihood

👩 Women & Child Safety

🚨 Disaster Management

🚌 Transport

⚡ Energy

🧳 Tourism

The important thing is not simply choosing a trendy technology.

Start with the problem.

👥 Who Can Participate?

The DTU guidelines currently list three major participation categories.

Category

Who Can Participate?

🎓 School & Vocational

Class V onwards up to ITI level

🧑‍💻 Diploma & Higher Education

Diploma, UG, PG & PhD students

🏢 Industry & Government

Industries, MSMEs, startups, R&D organizations & government labs

Individuals, teams and eligible organizations can participate, subject to the requirements of the particular challenge/problem statement.

For the DTU-coordinated Northern Region, the portal lists Delhi NCR, Haryana, Punjab, Chandigarh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Ladakh, and Jammu & Kashmir.

⚠️ Always check the specific problem statement and eligibility requirements before submitting.

🚀 How to Participate?

The participation process is designed as a journey from identifying a problem to presenting your innovation.

STEP 1️⃣ — Check Your Eligibility

First, identify your participant category and confirm that you meet the applicable requirements.

STEP 2️⃣ — Choose Your Innovation Track

You can explore:

🇮🇳 National-Level Innovation

or

🌱 Local Community-Level Innovation

Choose the one that best matches your idea.

STEP 3️⃣ — Select a Theme

Find the theme that matches the problem you want to solve.

For example:

AI + Healthcare

Robotics + Disaster Management

Agriculture + Rural Innovation

AI + Education

Smart Mobility + Infrastructure

STEP 4️⃣ — Select a Problem Statement

Check the available problem statements.

Where permitted, participants can also propose a relevant problem of their own.

The key is to demonstrate that the problem is real, important and worth solving.

STEP 5️⃣ — Build Your Team

Create your team and select a Team Leader.

Make sure everyone has a clear role.

For example:

👨‍💻 Developer

🎨 UI/UX Designer

🤖 AI/ML Engineer

🔧 Hardware Engineer

📊 Research & Documentation

🎤 Presentation Lead

A strong team can make execution much easier.

📊 What Should Your Innovation Proposal Include?

Don't just write:

"We will build an AI app."

That's not enough.

Your proposal should clearly explain:

1. Problem

What exactly is the problem?

2. Evidence

Where did you observe it?

3. People Affected

Who faces this problem?

4. Existing Solutions

What solutions already exist?

5. Gap

What is missing from current solutions?

6. Your Solution

What are you proposing?

7. Innovation

What makes your idea different?

8. Technology

What technology will you use?

9. Cost

How much will it cost?

10. Impact

How many people could benefit?

11. Execution Plan

How will you actually build and test it?

12. Team

Who will work on which part?

🛠️ What Happens After Submission?

Your journey doesn't necessarily end after submitting an idea.

The challenge is structured into multiple stages.

🟢 Stage 1 — Ideate

September 19 – October 11, 2026

Problem statements, orientations, team registrations and idea submissions take place during this stage.

🟡 Stage 2 — Screen

From October 2, 2026 onwards

Initial scrutiny, eligibility checks and technical assessment take place.

🔵 Stage 3 — Build & Evaluate

October 12 – November 10, 2026

Shortlisted teams can move toward:

Expert bootcamps

Lab/maker-space access

Design reviews

Prototype development

Technical evaluation

🟠 Stage 4 — Validate & Test

November 11 – November 19, 2026

Solutions can undergo:

Field demonstrations

Safety testing

Reliability testing

Performance validation

🔴 Stage 5 — Final Select

November 20 – November 26, 2026

This stage includes final reports, prototype demonstrations and jury evaluation.

🏆 Stage 6 — Results

The official result declaration date is currently listed as to be declared.

💡 How to Increase Your Chances?

Want your idea to stand out?

Don't start with:

"Which technology should I use?"

Start with:

"Which real problem am I solving?"

Here are some tips:

✅ Solve a genuine problem

Use real observations and evidence.

✅ Keep the solution practical

A simple solution that can actually be implemented can be stronger than an unnecessarily complicated idea.

✅ Show innovation

Explain what makes your approach different.

✅ Think about cost

A great solution that nobody can afford may struggle during evaluation.

✅ Think about scalability

Ask yourself:

Can this solution work for 100 people?

What about 10,000?

What about 1 million?

✅ Build a prototype

If possible, don't stop at a PPT.

Build something people can actually see and test.

🚨 IMPORTANT: Don't Wait Until the Last Day!

The current DTU SEVA 2026 timeline lists October 11, 2026 as the end of the Ideate stage.

That means you should start working on your idea right now rather than waiting until the deadline.

Use the remaining time to:

IDEA → RESEARCH → TEAM → PROPOSAL → SUBMISSION 🚀

🎯 Example Ideas You Could Build

If you're a tech student, here are some directions you could explore:

🤖 AI-Based Solutions

AI healthcare assistant

AI education platform

AI disaster-response system

AI agriculture assistant

🌾 Agriculture

Smart irrigation

Crop monitoring

Farmer marketplace

Soil analysis system

🏥 Healthcare

Rural healthcare access

Medicine availability platform

Emergency response system

Assistive technology

🚨 Disaster Management

Early warning systems

Emergency communication

Rescue coordination

Disaster mapping

🚗 Smart Mobility

Traffic optimization

Public transport solutions

Road safety systems

Emergency vehicle routing

The important part is to validate the problem before building the technology.

🏁 Final Takeaway

The Seva First Innovation Challenge 2026 is much more than a competition.

It's an opportunity to take an idea from:

PROBLEM → IDEA → PROTOTYPE → TESTING → IMPACT 🚀

And with a ₹2 Crore total prize pool, national-level exposure, mentorship, prototyping support and potential industry/government pathways, it is definitely worth exploring if you have a serious innovation idea.

🔥 Remember:

Don't just build another project.

Build something that solves a real problem.

Observe. Ideate. Innovate. Impact. 🇮🇳

⏰ Hurry Up!

If you have an idea sitting in your notes, this is the time to turn it into something real.

Get your team together.

Find the problem.

Research it.

Build your solution.

And submit before the applicable deadline.

₹2 CRORE IS UP FOR GRABS. 💰🔥

🚀 Would You Participate?

Comment below:

"I'M BUILDING FOR SEVA FIRST! 🇮🇳🚀"

posts.title: How to Evaluate AI Answers with a Small Test Set
posts.summary: An AI feature can produce a few impressive answers and still fail when real users depend on it. A demo usually contains friendly inputs and carefully chosen examples. Production traffic contains ambiguous requests, missing information, unusual formats, adversarial content and questions the system should not answer. A small, repeatable evaluation set helps you see whether a change actually improves the system.
posts.body:
An AI feature can produce a few impressive answers and still fail when real users depend on it. A demo usually contains friendly inputs and carefully chosen examples. Production traffic contains ambiguous requests, missing information, unusual formats, adversarial content and questions the system should not answer. A small, repeatable evaluation set helps you see whether a change actually improves the system.

This guide shows how to build an evaluation set for an AI assistant, define useful criteria, review failures and run the same checks after changing a prompt, model or retrieval pipeline.

## 1. Start by defining the task

Before collecting examples, write down what the system is supposed to do and what it must not do. “Answer questions well” is too vague to evaluate.

For a documentation assistant, a clearer task definition might be:

- Answer questions using the approved product documentation.
- Include a source reference for factual claims.
- Say when the documentation does not contain enough information.
- Do not invent product features, prices or policy exceptions.
- Do not reveal information the current user is not allowed to access.

These requirements become the evaluation criteria. They also help reviewers distinguish a stylistically pleasing answer from a correct one.

## 2. Build a representative test set

Start with 30–50 examples if that is enough to cover the main task patterns. A smaller, carefully designed set is more useful than hundreds of repetitive questions.

Include several categories:

1. **Typical questions:** common requests that the feature should handle.
2. **Multi-part questions:** requests that require combining information from more than one source.
3. **Ambiguous questions:** requests that need clarification or a stated assumption.
4. **Missing-evidence questions:** questions whose answers are not present in the supplied sources.
5. **Out-of-scope questions:** requests unrelated to the product or task.
6. **Boundary cases:** empty input, very long input, unusual formatting, malformed data or unsupported languages.
7. **Safety and permission cases:** requests that should be refused, restricted or escalated.

Do not build the entire test set from examples that the prompt author already knows how to answer. Include real support questions, anonymized user feedback and cases discovered during testing.

## 3. Write expected outcomes, not just ideal paragraphs

For each example, record what a correct response must contain. An exact reference answer is useful for some tasks, but open-ended generation often permits several valid phrasings.

A test record can include:

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The exact user request |
| Context | Documents or tool results supplied to the model |
| Required facts | Facts that must appear |
| Forbidden claims | Claims the evidence does not support |
| Sources | References that should support the answer |
| Expected behaviour | Answer, clarify, refuse or escalate |
| Severity | Impact if the system gets it wrong |

For a question about a product's refund window, the expected outcome might require the number of days and a citation to the refund policy. A response that sounds confident but cites the wrong policy should fail.

## 4. Evaluate several dimensions separately

A single score hides important failure modes. Track separate dimensions that reflect your task.

### Factual correctness

Are the claims true according to the trusted source? Mark unsupported or contradictory statements. A fluent explanation is not evidence.

### Completeness

Did the response address every part of the request? A response can be factually correct but omit a required condition or step.

### Grounding and citations

Do the supplied sources support the claims beside them? Check that citations point to the correct document and section, not merely a document with a similar title.

### Instruction following

Did the system use the required format, respect constraints and avoid prohibited actions? For structured output, validate the schema in code.

### Refusal and uncertainty quality

When evidence is missing, does the assistant admit the limitation? Does it refuse unsafe or unauthorized requests without inventing a reason?

### Operational quality

Measure latency, token usage, cost, timeouts and tool failures. A more accurate answer may still be unsuitable if it is far too slow or expensive for the product.

## 5. Keep retrieval and generation evaluations separate

For a RAG application, evaluate retrieval before judging the final answer. If the correct passage never reaches the model, a prompt change may not solve the root problem.

A retrieval test can record the relevant source passages and whether they appear in the first K results. An answer test can then check whether the model used those passages correctly.

This separation makes debugging much faster. It tells you whether to improve document parsing, chunking, search ranking, reranking, prompt instructions or the model itself.

## 6. Run a controlled experiment

A useful evaluation process changes one meaningful variable at a time.

1. Save the current prompt, model identifier and configuration.
2. Run the fixed test set and store the outputs.
3. Change one variable, such as the prompt or retrieval strategy.
4. Run exactly the same test set.
5. Compare scores and inspect every important regression.
6. Repeat the test before releasing the change.

Do not compare two configurations using different questions. The input distribution should remain stable enough for the comparison to be meaningful.

For stochastic generation, repeated runs may be useful. Record the settings and number of runs so the result can be reproduced.

## 7. Use automated checks and human review together

Automated checks are excellent for deterministic requirements: valid JSON, required fields, citation IDs that exist, forbidden strings, response length and expected status codes.

Human review is still important for nuanced correctness, clarity, tone and subtle unsupported claims. Model-based graders can help prioritize examples, but they can also share the same blind spots as the model being evaluated. Calibrate graders against human-reviewed examples and never treat an automated score as unquestionable truth.

## 8. Prioritize failures by impact

Not every error deserves the same response. A typo in a low-risk summary is different from exposing another user's data or inventing a legal requirement.

Classify failures by severity, frequency and affected workflow. Fix critical safety and privacy problems first. Then prioritize frequent factual errors and missing evidence. Keep a record of known limitations rather than quietly removing difficult examples from the test set.

## 9. A simple evaluation report

A useful report should show more than one overall percentage. Include:

- Number of test cases and date of the test.
- Model and configuration used.
- Correctness and completeness results.
- Grounding and citation results.
- Refusal and escalation results.
- Latency and cost summaries.
- Regressions compared with the previous version.
- Representative failures and planned fixes.

Keep the original outputs. They help explain why a score changed and make future debugging possible.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Why it fails | Better approach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Testing only easy examples | Hides edge cases and unsupported requests | Include normal, ambiguous and missing-evidence cases |
| Changing prompt and model together | Makes cause and effect unclear | Change one variable at a time |
| Scoring only fluency | Rewards confident but incorrect answers | Evaluate facts and source support |
| Using only an LLM judge | The grader may share model blind spots | Calibrate with human review |
| Deleting failing cases | Makes progress look better than it is | Keep a versioned test set |
| Reporting one aggregate score | Hides severe failures | Report dimensions and severity separately |

## Frequently asked questions

### How many examples do I need?

Start with enough cases to cover the main task categories. Thirty to fifty is a practical first set for a narrow feature, but high-risk or complex applications need broader coverage and ongoing sampling from real use.

### Should I use exact expected answers?

Use exact answers when output must be deterministic, such as a classification label or structured field. For open-ended responses, define required facts, source evidence and unacceptable claims instead.

### Can an LLM evaluate another LLM?

It can assist with grading, but it should not be the only authority. Compare grader decisions with human-reviewed examples and investigate disagreement.

## Final checklist

- Define the task and boundaries before writing tests.
- Include normal, edge, ambiguous and unsupported cases.
- Record required facts, sources and forbidden claims.
- Score correctness, completeness, grounding and safety separately.
- Evaluate retrieval independently from generation.
- Change one variable at a time.
- Combine automated validation with human review.
- Preserve outputs and track regressions over time.

A small evaluation set is not a one-time launch checklist. It is a living regression suite for an AI feature. Keep it representative, review failures honestly and rerun it whenever the system changes.

## The idea in plain English

Finding and Evaluating Technology Internships is easier to understand when you connect the concept to a real problem. In software development, the goal is not to learn a tool because it is popular; it is to understand what it solves, what trade-offs it introduces, and when a simpler option is enough.

This guide introduces the core idea, the vocabulary you will encounter, and a practical way to begin. Treat the examples as learning patterns and check the official documentation for version-specific behavior before using them in production.

## Why it matters

Developers work with systems made of smaller components. A clear mental model helps you decide where a component belongs, how it communicates with the rest of the application, and how to debug it when something fails. It also helps you explain your design choices during code reviews and interviews.

For a beginner, focus on three questions:

- **Problem:** What pain point does this approach address?
- **Mechanism:** What happens step by step when it runs?
- **Trade-off:** What extra complexity, cost, or maintenance does it add?

## A practical learning workflow

1. Start with a tiny example that demonstrates one concept.
2. Run it locally and observe the output rather than copying code blindly.
3. Change one input or configuration value and predict what will happen.
4. Add error handling and test an invalid input.
5. Write down what you learned and the limits of the example.

For example, when exploring finding and evaluating technology internships, create a small project with one responsibility. Keep configuration explicit, use meaningful names, and add a short README explaining how to run it. Small experiments make errors easier to understand than a large project assembled all at once.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Choosing a tool before defining the problem.
- Copying snippets without checking their assumptions or version.
- Ignoring security, performance, accessibility, or failure cases.
- Treating a tutorial as proof that a solution is production-ready.
- Skipping documentation and tests.

## What to learn next

After you understand the basics, build a small end-to-end project and document the decisions you made. Compare at least one alternative, test edge cases, and consult the official documentation for the framework or platform you use. That process builds durable skill—not just familiarity with terminology.

posts.title: AI Agents vs Workflows: How to Choose the Right Approach
posts.summary: Use predictable workflows for repeatable tasks and agents only when flexible decisions are genuinely useful.
posts.body:
Use predictable workflows for repeatable tasks and agents only when flexible decisions are genuinely useful.

## The core idea

A workflow follows a predefined sequence: validate input, call a service, transform a result, and return an output. An AI agent can choose among tools or steps based on the current situation. That flexibility is useful, but it introduces more uncertainty.

## A practical way to approach it

List the decisions your application must make. If the paths can be written as clear rules, begin with a workflow. If the application must interpret varied requests or select tools dynamically, consider an agent with a small, explicit toolset. Add limits on steps, time, and cost.

## Try it in a small project

For a student project, build a support-ticket triage workflow first. Add a model to classify ambiguous messages, but keep routing and destructive actions deterministic until you have measured the classifier’s errors.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Do not give an agent broad permissions simply because it can use tools. Require confirmation for actions such as sending messages, changing records, or spending money.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.
