posts.title: Docker for Beginners
posts.summary: Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into an image that can be run as a container. It helps developers create more consistent environments across laptops, CI systems and servers. Instead of manually installing every dependency on every machine, a team can describe the environment and build an image from that definition.
posts.body:
Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into an image that can be run as a container. It helps developers create more consistent environments across laptops, CI systems and servers. Instead of manually installing every dependency on every machine, a team can describe the environment and build an image from that definition.

Containers are useful, but they are not magic virtual machines. Understanding images, containers, ports, volumes and environment variables will help you use Docker safely and avoid common development problems.

## 1. What is a container?

A container is an isolated process environment that uses the host operating system's kernel. It has its own filesystem view, process and network configuration, subject to the container runtime and operating system.

A virtual machine usually includes a guest operating system and virtualized hardware. Containers generally share the host kernel, which makes them lighter to start and run in many workloads. The isolation model is different, so containers should not be treated as an automatic security boundary for hostile code.

## 2. Image versus container

A Docker image is a packaged, read-only template containing application files, dependencies and metadata. A container is a running or stopped instance created from an image.

You can create multiple containers from the same image. Each container has its own writable layer and runtime configuration, while the image provides the common base.

Useful commands:

```bash
docker images
docker ps
docker ps -a
```

The first lists local images. The second lists running containers. The third includes stopped containers.

## 3. Write a simple Dockerfile

A Dockerfile describes how to build an image. For a basic Python application:

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
```

This example chooses a base image, sets a working directory, installs dependencies, copies application files and defines the default command. For a real service, pin and update base images deliberately, use a non-root user where practical, and avoid copying secrets into the image.

Build the image:

```bash
docker build -t task-api:dev .
```

Run it:

```bash
docker run --rm task-api:dev
```

The exact command depends on the application. A web server also needs a port mapping and possibly configuration.

## 4. Understand port mapping

A process inside a container listens on a container port. To access it from the host, publish a port:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 task-api:dev
```

The left side is the host port and the right side is the container port. The application must listen on an address reachable from outside the container, commonly 0.0.0.0, rather than only 127.0.0.1 inside the container.

Publishing a port makes a service reachable through the host's network interfaces according to the runtime and firewall configuration. Do not publish databases or admin interfaces publicly without authentication and network controls.

## 5. Understand volumes and persistent data

A container's writable layer is not the right place for important data that must survive container replacement. Volumes provide persistent storage managed by Docker, while bind mounts connect a host path to a container path.

Example named volume:

```bash
docker volume create database-data
docker run -d --name db \
  -v database-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16
```

The path shown is the standard data directory for that example image; verify the correct path for the exact image and version you use.

A bind mount can be useful during local development:

```bash
docker run --rm -it \
  -v "$PWD:/app" \
  -w /app \
  python:3.12-slim python app.py
```

Mounting source code is convenient, but mounting over a directory can hide files that were already present in the image. Understand which side owns the data and what happens when the container is removed.

## 6. Configure environment variables

Applications often need configuration such as a port, environment name or database URL. Environment variables can pass configuration at runtime:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -e APP_ENV=development \
  -e PORT=8000 \
  task-api:dev
```

Do not bake passwords or API keys into a Dockerfile or image layer. Use a secret manager or the deployment platform's secret facility for sensitive values. A local .env file should be excluded from version control.

Environment variables are configuration, not a complete secret-management system. Restrict who can inspect container configuration and logs.

## 7. Use Docker Compose for multi-service projects

A web application may need an API and a database. Docker Compose describes multiple services in one YAML file and starts them together.

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:example@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - database-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  database-data:
```

This is a learning example, not a production secret configuration. Compose service names can be used for service-to-service communication on the project network. A depends_on relationship does not necessarily mean the database is ready to accept connections; applications should retry safely or use health checks and readiness logic.

Start the stack with `docker compose up --build` and stop it with `docker compose down`. Removing named volumes requires an additional explicit option; understand that data-loss effect before using it.

## 8. Make images smaller and safer

Use a small, maintained base image where appropriate. Add a .dockerignore file to exclude unnecessary files such as local environments, Git metadata, caches and secrets.

For example:

```gitignore
.git
.venv
__pycache__
.env
node_modules
dist
```

Use multi-stage builds when build tools are not needed at runtime. Copy only the artifacts required by the final image. Run as a non-root user when the application supports it, scan images, update dependencies and avoid running unnecessary services inside one container.

## 9. Debug common problems

| Symptom | Possible cause | What to inspect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container exits immediately | Main process completed or crashed | docker logs and container exit code |
| Host cannot reach service | Port not published or app bound to localhost | Port mapping and listen address |
| Data disappears | Data stored only in container layer | Volume or bind mount configuration |
| Permission denied | Host/container user IDs differ | File ownership and container user |
| Image build is slow | Large build context or uncached steps | .dockerignore and Dockerfile order |
| API starts before database | Dependency is not ready | Health checks and retry logic |

Useful commands include `docker logs`, `docker inspect`, `docker exec -it CONTAINER sh`, and `docker compose ps`. Avoid placing secrets in commands that may be stored in shell history.

## 10. A practical learning project

Containerize a small API with one endpoint and a database. First build and run the API alone. Then publish its port, add a persistent database volume, and configure the connection through environment variables. Rebuild the image after changing dependencies and verify that database data survives container replacement.

Document the exact commands in the README. Test the project from a clean clone to confirm that another developer can reproduce it.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is a Docker container the same as a virtual machine?

No. Containers share the host kernel and isolate processes and resources differently from a VM, which typically runs a guest operating system.

### Do containers keep data after they are removed?

Not reliably in their writable layer. Use a volume or bind mount for data that must persist.

### Should I put secrets in environment variables?

Environment variables are common for configuration, but secrets should be supplied through a suitable secret-management mechanism and protected from logs and unauthorized inspection.

## Final checklist

- Understand the difference between image and container.
- Use a Dockerfile to describe reproducible builds.
- Publish only the ports that need to be reachable.
- Use volumes for persistent data.
- Supply configuration at runtime.
- Keep secrets out of images and Git.
- Add .dockerignore and use multi-stage builds where useful.
- Add health checks, retries and monitoring for real services.

Docker becomes much easier when each concept has a clear job: images package software, containers run it, ports expose services, volumes persist data, and environment variables configure behaviour.

posts.title: REST APIs vs. GraphQL
posts.summary: REST and GraphQL are two common ways for applications to exchange data over HTTP. Both can support web and mobile products, but they organize requests differently. REST commonly exposes resources through multiple endpoints. GraphQL commonly exposes a typed schema through which a client asks for the fields it needs.
posts.body:
REST and GraphQL are two common ways for applications to exchange data over HTTP. Both can support web and mobile products, but they organize requests differently. REST commonly exposes resources through multiple endpoints. GraphQL commonly exposes a typed schema through which a client asks for the fields it needs.

Neither approach is automatically faster, safer or easier. The right choice depends on the shape of your data, client requirements, caching strategy, team experience and operational constraints.

## 1. Understand the REST approach

In a REST-style API, resources are represented by URLs and HTTP methods communicate the action. A student application might expose:

```http
GET /students/42
GET /students/42/courses
GET /courses/10
POST /students
PATCH /students/42
DELETE /students/42
```

The server defines the representation returned by each endpoint. HTTP semantics, status codes, caching headers and resource identifiers are important parts of a well-designed REST API.

REST is not simply “JSON over HTTP.” A good resource API uses predictable resource names, appropriate methods, meaningful status codes and consistent error responses.

## 2. Understand the GraphQL approach

GraphQL defines a schema of types and fields. A client sends a query describing the data it needs:

```graphql
query StudentProfile($id: ID!) {
  student(id: $id) {
    name
    courses {
      title
      grade
    }
  }
}
```

The server validates the query against the schema and resolves the requested fields. The client can ask for a nested result in one operation, rather than calling several REST endpoints and combining the responses itself.

GraphQL also supports mutations for changing data and subscriptions in implementations that provide a real-time transport. The schema is a contract, but it still needs authorization, validation and performance controls.

## 3. Over-fetching and under-fetching

With a fixed REST response, a client may receive fields it does not need. This is sometimes called over-fetching. A client may also need several requests to collect related resources, which can be described as under-fetching.

GraphQL allows clients to select fields, which can reduce unnecessary response data and combine related information. But it does not make every query efficient. A deeply nested query can trigger many database lookups or return far more data than expected.

The server must limit query depth, complexity, execution time and resource consumption where appropriate. Field selection is a client convenience, not a substitute for backend performance design.

## 4. Compare the main trade-offs

| Area | REST | GraphQL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request model | Resource-oriented endpoints | Schema and field-oriented operations |
| Response shape | Usually designed by each endpoint | Selected by the client within schema limits |
| Caching | HTTP caching can be straightforward for GET resources | Often needs a deliberate client/server caching strategy |
| Versioning | May use URL or header versioning | Schema evolution often uses field deprecation |
| Tooling | Widely supported HTTP tools | Schema-aware tools and GraphQL clients |
| Complexity | Familiar resource and endpoint design | Requires schema, resolver and query governance |
| Best fit | Stable resource APIs and broad compatibility | Clients with varied data needs and connected data graphs |

This table is a starting point, not a universal ranking. REST can be highly flexible, and GraphQL can be simple for a small schema. The implementation matters more than the label.

## 5. Caching and performance

REST GET requests fit naturally into standard HTTP caching patterns. A CDN or proxy can cache public responses when cache headers and authorization rules permit it. Cache keys and invalidation still need care, especially when responses vary by user or query parameters.

GraphQL commonly sends different queries to the same endpoint, so caching can require persisted queries, normalized client caches or server-side caching at the resolver or data layer. It is possible to cache GraphQL effectively, but the strategy should be designed rather than assumed.

For both approaches, measure database query counts, response size, latency and error rate. GraphQL resolvers can create the N+1 problem: one parent query is followed by a separate database request for each child. Batching and data-loader patterns can reduce this overhead.

## 6. Security considerations

Both styles need authentication and authorization. A user who can access a student record should not automatically be able to access every student's record.

For REST, enforce permissions on every resource and action. Do not rely on hiding a button in the frontend. Validate request bodies, query parameters and path identifiers, and use rate limits for expensive operations.

For GraphQL, authorization must be enforced at the appropriate resolver or data-access layer. Avoid assuming that a hidden field is protected simply because the client does not request it. Limit query depth and complexity, control introspection according to your threat model, and protect expensive nested operations.

Never expose internal stack traces, database credentials or sensitive fields in error messages.

## 7. When should you choose REST?

REST is a strong default when:

- The API maps naturally to stable resources.
- HTTP caching and standard tooling are important.
- Many external developers need a familiar interface.
- The application has straightforward CRUD workflows.
- The team wants a simple operational model.

A REST API can still provide filtering, pagination, sparse field selection and purpose-built endpoints. You do not need GraphQL merely because one screen needs data from two resources.

## 8. When should you choose GraphQL?

GraphQL can be useful when:

- Several clients need different combinations of the same data.
- The domain contains connected resources.
- Frontend teams need flexibility to evolve screen queries.
- A typed schema and introspection improve developer workflows.
- The organization can operate resolver performance and query governance.

It is especially valuable when clients otherwise make many coordinated requests or depend on large endpoint-specific response shapes.

## 9. A practical decision process

Start by listing the clients and the data each screen needs. Measure the number of requests, response sizes, cacheability and backend query costs. Then build a small representative endpoint or schema and compare implementation effort.

Ask:

1. Are resources and actions naturally represented by HTTP methods and URLs?
2. Do clients need substantially different response shapes?
3. Is caching a major requirement?
4. Can the team monitor and secure nested queries?
5. Are there existing API conventions that should remain stable?
6. What will versioning and backward compatibility look like?

Avoid migrating a working REST API to GraphQL solely because GraphQL is newer. Migration has costs, and a gateway or aggregation endpoint may solve the actual problem more simply.

## Common mistakes

- Treating GraphQL as automatically faster.
- Exposing every database field in a GraphQL schema.
- Ignoring N+1 queries and query complexity.
- Building REST endpoints that do not have clear resource semantics.
- Applying authorization only in the frontend.
- Forgetting caching, pagination, rate limiting and observability.
- Choosing a technology before understanding client requirements.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can REST and GraphQL coexist?

Yes. An organization can keep existing REST services and expose a GraphQL layer for clients that benefit from a connected schema. Use clear ownership and avoid duplicating business rules across layers.

### Is GraphQL a replacement for SQL?

No. GraphQL describes how clients request data from an API. The server may use SQL, NoSQL, other services or a combination behind its resolvers.

### Which is better for beginners?

REST is often a simpler starting point because HTTP methods, URLs and status codes are widely used. Learning GraphQL afterward helps you understand schema-driven APIs and client-controlled data selection.

## Final checklist

- Start with client and resource requirements.
- Design predictable responses and errors.
- Consider caching, pagination and performance early.
- Enforce authorization on the server.
- Protect expensive queries and operations.
- Measure real workloads before choosing or migrating.
- Document the API contract and deprecation policy.

REST and GraphQL are tools for different API design needs. Choose the approach that makes the system easiest to understand, secure, operate and evolve—not the one with the most fashionable name.

Progressive enhancement means the core content and navigation should remain understandable, while JavaScript improves the experience when available. This is especially valuable for simple content sites and forms.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

posts.title: What is an AI agent? A beginner-friendly guide
posts.summary: AI agents are everywhere in tech news. Here is a plain explanation of what they are, how they differ from chatbots, and how to start building one.
posts.body:
You have probably seen the phrase "AI agent" in the news and in Google Cloud's learning content. It sounds complicated, but the idea is simple.

## Chatbot versus agent

A chatbot answers your question and stops. An **AI agent** is given a goal, decides which steps to take, uses tools to carry them out, and keeps going until the goal is done or it needs your help.

For example, a chatbot can explain how to book a meeting room. An agent could check the calendar, pick a free slot, send the invite and tell you it is done.

## The main parts of an agent

- **A model:** the language model that reads instructions and decides what to do next.
- **Instructions:** a plain description of the agent's job and its limits.
- **Tools:** things the agent is allowed to use, such as searching a database, calling an API or reading a file.
- **A loop:** the agent thinks, acts, looks at the result, and repeats.

## Why "multi-agent" matters

Bigger systems often use several agents with different roles. One agent might gather data, another might check it, and a third might write the final answer. Google Skills has skill badges on exactly this, including engineering agents with the Agent Development Kit, deploying multi-agent architectures, and orchestrating multi-agent workflows.

## Keep agents on a short leash

Because an agent can take actions, it should only be given the access it truly needs. Read what it plans to do, test it on sample data first, and never share secrets you would not put in a document. Even the 2026 Arcade Facilitator bonus project asked learners to give access to a single verifier account rather than opening everything up.

## How to start building

1. Learn the basics with hands-on labs on [Google Skills](https://www.skills.google/).
2. Try the agent-related skill badges to see the tools in action.
3. Use the Google Cloud free trial for your own small project. Google describes it as 90 days with $300 in credits, and says it will not charge your card automatically when the trial ends.
4. Start with something tiny, like an agent that answers questions from a short document, and grow from there.

Read the next post to see how Google turned this into a real project for Arcade Facilitator learners: [Build your first AI agent on Google Cloud](first-ai-agent-google-cloud-bonus-milestone.html).

posts.title: Google Skills Arcade 2026 prize tiers explained: points, prize spots and the waterfall
posts.summary: The four 2026 Arcade prize tiers, how many prizes each one has, how the waterfall system works, and what changed from last year.
posts.body:
Google announced the Google Skills Arcade 2026 prize tiers on 10 June 2026. If you are collecting points this year, these are the numbers to plan around.

## The four tiers

| Tier | Arcade points | Prize spots |
|---|---|---|
| Trooper | 50 to 74 | 6,000 |
| Ranger | 75 to 94 | 4,000 |
| Champion | 95 to 119 | 3,000 |
| Legend | 120 or more | 2,500 |

## What is different this year

- **The Novice tier is gone.** Google says the season lasts a full year, so the rewards now focus on the four tiers above.
- **Each tier has a limit.** For the first time, only a set number of players can receive prizes in each tier. Google says the limits are well above the number of prizes claimed last year.

## How the waterfall works

The Prize Counter works on a first come, first served basis, starting at the Legend tier. Suppose you have 120 or more points but the 2,500 Legend spots are already taken. Your points then move you to the front of the line for Champion prizes. If Champion is full, you roll down to Ranger, and then to Trooper.

The practical lesson is simple: the earlier you lock in your points, the higher up the waterfall you stay.

## When do the prizes arrive?

The Prize Counter is due to open shortly after the 2026 season ends at the end of the year. Google also said in April that all the Arcade points you have earned during 2026 are safe and will count when the counter opens.

## Where the points come from

- **Arcade games:** one point each. Since April 2026 every game is worth the same.
- **Skill badges:** half a point each, so two badges make one point.
- **Facilitator program:** bonus points from milestones. The 2026 program ran from 13 July to 14 September.

## Work out where you stand

Type your numbers into the [Arcade Points Calculator](../arcade-calculator.html) to see your current tier, what you still need for the next one, and what a steady pace could give you by the end of the year.

> Rules can change, so always confirm the details on Google's official announcement: [Google Skills Arcade 2026 Tiers](https://discuss.google.dev/t/google-skills-arcade-2026-tiers/371066). Points and tiers on this website are estimates.

- be enrolled in the Arcade Facilitator 2026 cohort
- hold both the GEAR badge and the Arcade GEAR badge on your Google Developer Profile
- have unlocked Milestone 1 in the Facilitator program

### 1. Finish four GEAR skill badges

- Create Your First Gemini Enterprise Application
- Engineer AI Agents with ADK
- Deploy Multi-Agent Architectures
- Orchestrate Multi-agent Workflows

Google noted that these also counted toward the normal Arcade milestones, so the work paid off twice.

### 2. Start your Google Cloud free trial

Learners signed up for the 90-day trial with $300 in credits, using the email address enrolled in the program. Anyone who already had an active billing account on that email could skip this step.

### 3. Build the agent

Follow the project instructions to build your first agent with Google Cloud's Vertex AI platform. The last step is to give access to the verifier email address so your project can be checked.

### 4. Submit your details

Fill in the verification form with your Project ID and your 18-character Billing Account ID from the Google Cloud console.

## Tips from the community

Several learners in Google's forum reported problems setting up billing during the trial sign-up, so start early and read Google's free trial FAQs if something fails.

## Why this project is worth copying

Building a real agent teaches more than watching a demo. If you want the ideas behind it first, read [What is an AI agent?](what-is-an-ai-agent-beginner-guide.html). To see how those 10 points fit into your prize tier, use the [Arcade Points Calculator](../arcade-calculator.html).

posts.title: A free roadmap to learn Google Cloud as a beginner in 2026
posts.summary: A simple step-by-step plan to start learning Google Cloud for free with Google Skills, Arcade games, skill badges and small projects.
posts.body:
Google Cloud can look huge when you are starting out. This roadmap breaks it into small steps you can follow for free, one at a time.

## Step 1: Create your Google Skills account

Google Skills is where the hands-on labs, courses and skill badges live. Sign up on [skills.google](https://www.skills.google/) and set up your public profile so your badges are recorded.

## Step 2: Play the monthly Arcade games

Each month the Google Skills Arcade releases new hands-on games. Every game is worth one Arcade point, and the access code for each game is on the official Arcade page. Games are short, so they are a friendly way to get used to the console.

## Step 3: Earn skill badges

Skill badges go deeper than games. Each badge is worth half an Arcade point, and together they build proof of your skills. Pick a theme and stay with it for a while, for example storage and data, or AI and agents, rather than jumping between topics.

## Step 4: Use the free trial for your own projects

Google offers a 90-day trial with $300 in credits, and says it will not charge your card automatically when the trial ends. Use it for small projects that are not part of a lab.

## Step 5: Build tiny projects

After each topic, build something small on your own:

- store files in Cloud Storage
- deploy a simple app to Cloud Run
- query a sample dataset in BigQuery
- try a Vertex AI example

## Step 6: Take notes and repeat

Write down commands, mistakes and useful links after every lab. Try repeating a lab from memory a few days later. Thirty to sixty minutes a day beats one huge weekend.

## Step 7: Join the community

The [Google Developer forums](https://discuss.google.dev/c/google-cloud/14) are full of learners sharing tips and asking questions.

## Track your progress

Keep count of your games and badges with the [Arcade Points Calculator](../arcade-calculator.html). It has a checklist that remembers your progress and shows which prize tier you are heading for.

Want to see these steps done live? Watch the walkthroughs on the [B Tecky YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCS9BcPpwy1W5Xorp0KU23aQ).

posts.title: How to check your Arcade score on B Tecky (no login)
posts.summary: Step by step: use the free B Tecky Arcade Score Checker to see your points, milestone and rank from your email.
posts.body:
The [Arcade Score Checker](../arcade.html) is a free tool on this website. You type the email you used for the Facilitator program and it shows where you stand. There is nothing to sign in to and nothing to install.

## How to use it

1. Open the [Arcade Score Checker](../arcade.html).
2. Type the email address linked to your Google Skills account.
3. Press **Check my score**.
4. Read your estimated total, your milestone and your rank, and see which games and skill badges are counted.

## What you will see

- Your **estimated total points**, made from games, skill badges and milestone bonuses.
- Your **milestone**, and how far you are from the next one.
- Your **rank** among everyone in the report.
- The names of the arcade games and skill badges you have completed.

## Good to know

- Capital letters do not matter, and for Gmail addresses dots and `+tags` are ignored.
- Your email is matched inside your own browser. It is never sent to a server or saved.
- Scores come from a report with a date shown on the page, so newer progress may not appear until the report is refreshed.
- If your email is not found, check for typos and make sure you joined through the batches in that report.

Want to know how the points are worked out? Read [How Google Cloud Arcade points work](how-google-cloud-arcade-points-work.html).

posts.title: How Google Cloud Arcade points work (2026 Facilitator program)
posts.summary: A plain-English guide to arcade game points, skill badge points, milestone bonuses and the AI agent bonus in the 2026 Facilitator program.
posts.body:
If you are collecting points in the Google Cloud Arcade Facilitator program, it helps to know exactly where every point comes from. Here is the simple version.

## Points from games and skill badges

- **Arcade games:** each completed arcade game gives **1 point**. Since April 2026 every game is worth the same single point.
- **Skill badges:** every **2 skill badges** give **1 point**, so each badge is worth 0.5 points. Completing 18 badges is worth 9 points.

## Milestone bonuses

Reaching a milestone adds a bonus on top of your game and badge points. You only receive the bonus for the milestone you reach, not for the ones before it.

| Milestone | Arcade games | Skill badges | Bonus points |
|---|---|---|---|
| Milestone 1 | 6 | 18 | 5 |
| Milestone 2 | 8 | 34 | 15 |
| Milestone 3 | 10 | 50 | 25 |
| Ultimate Milestone | 12 | 66 | 35 |

## The AI agent bonus

There is also a bonus milestone for an AI agent project. Earning it adds **10 points**.

## A worked example

Say you have completed 7 arcade games and 24 skill badges, and you have reached Milestone 1.

- Games: 7 points
- Skill badges: 24 x 0.5 = 12 points
- Milestone 1 bonus: 5 points
- **Total: 24 points**

> The rules can change between programs, so always check the official Google Skills page for the latest details. Points shown on this website are estimates.

## Plan your points

Want to see your prize tier and what is left to earn? Use the [Arcade Points Calculator](../arcade-calculator.html). It adds up your games, badges and bonuses and shows how far you are from each tier.

## Check your Facilitator score

Enter your email in the free [Arcade Score Checker](../arcade.html) to see your estimated points, milestone and rank in seconds. No login is needed.

Want more walkthroughs? Subscribe to the [B Tecky channel](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCS9BcPpwy1W5Xorp0KU23aQ).

posts.title: Coding agents are changing AI research: what OpenAI reported in September 2026
posts.summary: OpenAI shared an inside look at how coding agents are being used by its researchers, including changes in experiment workflows and task complexity.
posts.body:
OpenAI published a September 2026 report describing how coding agents are being used inside its research organisation. The report focuses on research workflows rather than presenting coding agents as a replacement for researchers. ## What changed in the workflow OpenAI says researchers are writing more code and running more experiments with the help of coding agents. It also describes a shift in the kinds of tasks agents are used for, as researchers become more comfortable delegating parts of technical workflows. That matters because AI-assisted programming is increasingly about more than autocomplete. Coding agents can help with multi-step tasks such as exploring a codebase, writing changes, running experiments and iterating on results. ## What developers should take from it The useful takeaway for students is not simply “use an AI coding agent.” Instead, learn a workflow where you remain responsible for the result: 1. Give the agent a small, well-defined task. 2. Ask it to explain assumptions before making risky changes. 3. Review the generated code. 4. Run tests and inspect failures. 5. Keep sensitive credentials and production access out of the agent's reach. ## Why this trend matters Coding agents are becoming part of the software-development toolchain. That makes fundamentals such as Git, debugging, testing, system design and code review even more useful because they give developers the ability to verify what an agent produces. ## Source - OpenAI: Research acceleration — the view inside OpenAI

Published 6 September 2026. This post summarises OpenAI's own report and its stated observations about internal research workflows.
